doc.title: Joanne Brackeen interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 10, 2001

title: Audiences in New York and Europe
summary: She plays the Jazz Standard and small clubs in New York and compares receptive European audiences, seeing it all as one music.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Do you find it different overseas as far as the audience for your music?

Well I haven’t had too many calls to do that music — no I can’t say that, I do do that. I worked at the Jazz Standard every year here and then I kind of work some subterranean clubs because I like to do that. So one club is, they get so many people in the club that they don’t advertise.

It’s fun, yeah. And I do that maybe two or three times a year, and then I worked in the main club, the Jazz Standard. We get great reception now. We get great reception also in Europe. So it’s hard to say. Sometimes in the European audiences, I mean you can tell they haven’t heard this kind of music, whereas in New York it’s a great audience, but they are a little more sophisticated — maybe less jumping up and down and like little kids in Europe. That’s great but I can’t say that one is more appreciative than the other. I think that there’s a lot of appreciation. The one thing that does seem to happen more in Europe is there are more venues per the population so the sense of culture and art is, and it’s a much older country, they developed more. But we have just great music here. I still prefer our music. You know, our musicians, our music. I was reading articles and hearing
people saying oh the music here is becoming like kind of backwards and it’s more creative in Europe. But I don’t join that. I’m kind of international. I see it all as one thing.
The term “world music” has entered kind of just as a phrase. And it’s amazing how fast things get spread around now with communication. And I like to think of our music as world music too.
Well it is. It is. I know those computers, they really do something.
